Let

\[
S=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\left(2^{-\lfloor 101k/1\rfloor}+2^{-\lfloor 101k/2\rfloor}+\cdots+2^{-\lfloor 101k/100\rfloor}\right).
\]

Set \(x=2^{-1}\). Since all terms are nonnegative, we may sum over \(j=1,\dots,100\) first:

\[
S=\sum_{j=1}^{100}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}x^{\lfloor 101k/j\rfloor}.
\]

For fixed \(j\), write every positive integer \(k\) uniquely as

\[
k=qn+r,\qquad n\ge 0,\quad 1\le r\le j.
\]

Then

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{101k}{j}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor 101n+\frac{101r}{j}\right\rfloor
=
101n+\left\lfloor \frac{101r}{j}\right\rfloor.
\]

Thus

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}x^{\lfloor 101k/j\rfloor}
=
\left(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^{101n}\right)
\left(\sum_{r=1}^{j}x^{\lfloor 101r/j\rfloor}\right)
=
\frac{\sum_{r=1}^{j}x^{\lfloor 101r/j\rfloor}}{1-x^{101}}.
\]

Therefore

\[
S=\frac{1}{1-2^{-101}}
\sum_{j=1}^{100}\sum_{r=1}^{j}2^{-\lfloor 101r/j\rfloor}.
\]

Now evaluate the finite double sum. Let \(N_m\) be the number of pairs \((j,r)\) with \(1\le r\le j\le 100\) such that

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{101r}{j}\right\rfloor=m.
\]

Since \(1\le r/j\le 1\), the possible values of \(m\) are \(1,2,\dots,101\).

For fixed \(m\), the condition is

\[
mj\le 101r<(m+1)j.
\]

For \(1\le m\le 100\), the interval length is \(j/101<1\), so there is at most one integer \(r\).

Write

\[
mj=101q+t,\qquad 1\le t\le 100,
\]

where \(t\equiv mj\pmod{101}\). The interval becomes

\[
q+\frac{t}{101}\le r<q+\frac{t+j}{101}.
\]

The only possible integer is \(q+1\), and it lies in the interval exactly when

\[
t+j>101.
\]

Now consider the pairing

\[
j\longleftrightarrow 101-j.
\]

If \(t\equiv mj\pmod{101}\), then for \(j'=101-j\),

\[
t'\equiv m(101-j)\equiv -mj\pmod{101},
\]

so \(t'=101-t\). Hence

\[
t'+j'=101-t+101-j=202-(t+j).
\]

Thus \(t+j>101\) for one of the pair \(\{j,101-j\}\) exactly when the other has \(t+j<101\). For \(1\le m\le 99\), equality \(t+j=101\) would imply

\[
mj\equiv -j\pmod{101}\implies (m+1)j\equiv 0\pmod{101},
\]

impossible because \(101\) is prime and \(1\le m+1,j\le 100\). Therefore each of the \(50\) pairs contributes exactly one valid \(j\), so

\[
N_m=50\qquad (1\le m\le 99).
\]

For \(m=100\), \(t=101-j\), so \(t+j=101\) always, and no integer \(r\) exists; hence \(N_{100}=0\). For \(m=101\), we must have \(r=j\), which works for every \(j\), so

\[
N_{101}=100.
\]

Therefore

\[
\sum_{j=1}^{100}\sum_{r=1}^{j}2^{-\lfloor 101r/j\rfloor}
=
50\sum_{m=1}^{99}2^{-m}+100\cdot 2^{-101}.
\]

Since

\[
\sum_{m=1}^{99}2^{-m}=1-2^{-99},
\]

the finite double sum equals

\[
50(1-2^{-99})+100\cdot 2^{-101}
=
50-100\cdot 2^{-101}.
\]

Hence

\[
S=\frac{50-100\cdot 2^{-101}}{1-2^{-101}}.
\]

Multiplying numerator and denominator by \(2^{101}\),

\[
S=\frac{50\cdot 2^{101}-100}{2^{101}-1}
=\frac{100(2^{100}-1)}{2^{101}-1}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{100(2^{100}-1)}{2^{101}-1}}
\]
